question.text:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

\[ A = \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{matrix}\right], \qquad B = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{matrix}\right], \qquad C = \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right] \]
question.explanation:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I_2$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_2:=(-2)R_2,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} && R_2:= (-2)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= A \end{align*}

  • The matrix $B$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I_2$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

  • The matrix $C$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I_2$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1: = R_1+(-1) R_2,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} && R_1: = R_1+(-1) R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= C \end{align*}

Therefore, only $A$ and $C$ are elementary matrices.

question.text:
Which of the following are not elementary matrices?

\[ H = \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 \end{matrix}\right],\qquad K = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{matrix}\right],\qquad N = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{matrix}\right] \]
question.explanation:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • The matrix $H$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I_2$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_2:= R_2 + 5 R_1,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} && R_2:= R_2 + 5 R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 5 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= H \end{align*}

  • The matrix $K$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I_2$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} && R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= K \end{align*}

  • The matrix $N$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I_2$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

Therefore, only $N$ is not an elementary matrix.

question.explanation:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • The matrix $A$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I_2$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_2:=R_1+ R_2,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} && R_1:=R_1+ R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= A \end{align*}

  • The matrix $B$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I_2$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1\leftrightarrow R_2,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} && R_1\leftrightarrow R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= B \end{align*}

  • The matrix $C$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I_2$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

Therefore, only $A$ and $B$ are elementary matrices.

question.text:
Which of the following are elementary matrices?

\[ T = \left[ \begin{matrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{matrix}\right],\qquad U = \left[ \begin{matrix} 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right],\qquad X = \left[ \begin{matrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{matrix}\right] \]
question.explanation:
An elementary matrix is a matrix obtained from the identity matrix by applying exactly one elementary row operation.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices.

  • The matrix $T$ is not an elementary matrix because it can't be obtained from $I_2$ by applying only one elementary row operation.

  • The matrix $U$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I_2$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1 := 9R_1,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} && R_1 := 9R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= U \end{align*}

  • The matrix $X$ is an elementary matrix because it can be obtained from $I_2$ by applying the elementary row operation $R_1:= R_1 +3 R_2,$ as follows: \begin{align*} I_2 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} && R_1 := R_1 +3 R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= X \end{align*}

Therefore, only $U$ and $X$ are elementary matrices.

question.text: Find the inverse of the elementary matrix $ Q = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -\dfrac{1}{7} \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. $
question.explanation:
We write down $Q$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

\begin{align*} [Q\,|\,I \,] & = \left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & -\dfrac{1}{7} & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] && R_1:= R_1+\dfrac{1}{7}R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & \dfrac{1}{7} \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

The inverse is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,

\[ Q^{-1}= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \dfrac{1}{7} \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

exampleAnswers.title: Computing a Product Involving the Inverse of an Elementary 2x2 Matrix

question.text: Find the product $E^{-1}_1 E_{2}$, where \begin{align*} E_1 &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1\\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad E_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}
question.explanation:
Notice that $E_1$ and $E_2$ are both elementary matrices.

First, we need to find $E_1^{-1}.$ We write down $E_1$ and the identity matrix $I$ side-by-side (as shown below) and apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix:

\begin{align*} [E_1\,|\,I \,] & = \left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] && R_1:= R_1 + R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

Therefore, \[ E_1^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, we can find the product $E_1^{-1} E_{2}\mathbin{:}$

\[ E^{-1}_1 E_{2} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1\\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]
